sections.html:
In Medina you can work with a broker, handle the sale yourself, or accept an offer from someone who will buy the house as it stands. All three finish the same way: a deed at the Medina County Auditor and a filing at the recorder.

Your timeline and the house's condition usually settle the question. Listing can bring several offers, along with showings, inspection findings and a contract that depends on the buyer's loan. A cash purchase narrows the process to one conversation about price and closing date.

  • List with an agent: broader reach, plus commission and repair negotiations.
  • Go it alone: you set the price and run the process.
  • Sell for cash: one negotiated offer for the house in its current state.

Medina has an estimated 25,692 residents as of July 1, 2025, down 1.5 percent from a 2020 base of 26,075. Owner-occupied homes have a 2020-2024 median value of $243,600, and owners live in 67.3 percent of units.

Median gross rent is $1,077 and median household income is $77,385. There are 10,911 households at 2.33 people apiece, and 92.1 percent of residents stayed in the same home over the prior year, which points to a stable, owner-minded market. Land area is 11.58 square miles, so lots near the Square are tight.

Medina's center is a historic district, so older homes near the Square sit in a place that works to preserve its look. A Community Design Committee and a Historic Preservation Board look after the historic character, and the district covers a nine-block area around Uptown Park.

The Square dates to rebuilding after two fires. An 1848 blaze destroyed the whole business district, and an 1870 fire destroyed 45 buildings. It took almost ten years to replace them, which is why Victorian style is so common there. Medina was founded in 1818 and chartered as a city in 1952.

For a house in or near the district, check with the city on whether exterior work needs review, and do that before promising a buyer any changes.

The city lies about 33 miles south of Cleveland and 23 miles west of Akron, spread across parts of Lafayette, Medina, Montville and York townships. Many residents commute to Cleveland and Akron, and the average trip to work takes 24.3 minutes. RPM International is among the companies based in town.

The Medina City School District serves the city. Its schools include Medina High School, A.I. Root and Claggett middle schools, and the elementary schools Ella Canavan, H.G. Blake, Sidney Fenn, Eliza Northrop and Ralph E. Waite. Garfield and Heritage elementary schools closed at the end of the 2023-24 school year after redistricting.

Private options include St. Francis Xavier School and Medina Christian Academy.

The city's Building Department handles plan review, inspections and property maintenance enforcement, and it tries to link owners of run-down properties with assistance programs and volunteer groups. You can reach it at 330-722-9030.

Ohio's 2024 Building, Mechanical and Plumbing Codes took effect March 1, 2024, and the department holds every application received after that date to those requirements. Ask the city's Planning Department any zoning questions about a lot or an outbuilding.

After a finished basement, a new deck or replaced mechanicals, ask the department whether the permits were closed out. A buyer's inspector will ask too, and a cash buyer will price any gap.

Medina County's real property conveyance fee is $3.00 for every $1,000 of sale price. The auditor rounds a price up to the next $100 when it ends in a fraction, and an online calculator on the auditor's site gives an estimate.

The auditor's site separates taxable conveyances from exempt ones and posts a form for each.

Medina County auditor transfer forms
FormUse it for
DTE 100Statement of value on a taxable sale
DTE 100EXStating the reason a transfer is exempt
Farm-use valuation statementLand in the farm-use valuation program

Check with the auditor on how the current rate applies to your sale before you settle on a price. The seller normally pays it, so build it into your net.

More than two dozen exemption reasons appear on the county's list, and many involve families and estates. Examples:

  • Gifts from one spouse to another, or from parent to child.
  • Passing to an heir or devisee, to a surviving spouse, or on a registered owner's death.
  • Moves where no value changes hands and no gift is involved.
  • Into a trust the grantor can freely revoke.
  • Under a court order, to the extent the transfer is not a sale carried out under that order.
  • Sales to cover delinquent taxes or assessments.

An exempt transfer still needs paperwork. Ohio Revised Code 319.202 swaps the full value statement for a short statement of the exemption reason.

A rental parcel needs a contact filing at the county auditor, with updates due 60 days after any change (Ohio Revised Code 5323.02). The auditor's endorsement on a rental deed points the new owner to that filing.

Bring up the tenants and the lease in your first talk with a buyer. Keep records of deposits and rent already paid, and agree in writing who returns deposits and when tenants must move out.

sections.h2: When a cash offer suits you
sections.html:
Cash makes sense when you value certainty over the widest possible market. In Medina that can include owners with historic-district houses that need expensive work, heirs who live away, and landlords who want out of a rental.

  • Ask what the buyer assumes: as-is condition, closing costs, move-out date.
  • Compare the figure to a listing net after repairs, commission and carrying costs.
  • Read the contract for who pays the conveyance fee and recording charges.

sections.h2: From signed contract to recorded deed
sections.html: Once you have a signed contract, ask a title company or attorney to prepare the deed, and order a payoff letter if you owe on a mortgage. Decide whether the sale is taxable or exempt, then complete DTE 100 or DTE 100EX with the auditor. The auditor endorses the deed after fees are paid, and the recorder files it. Any unpaid taxes and your payoff come out of the proceeds at closing, which a draft settlement statement will show ahead of time. With a cash buyer, no lender timeline sits behind these steps, so the date is easier to set around your move.

faqs.q: How much is the Medina County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The Medina County Auditor states $3.00 per $1,000 of the sale price. A sale price ending in a fraction of $100 is rounded up to the nearest $100, and the auditor offers an online calculator.

faqs.q: Does an inherited house in Medina owe the conveyance fee?
faqs.a: Usually not. The county exempts transfers to an heir or devisee and among heirs when no money is paid. The buyer or recipient still files the exemption statement, DTE 100EX.

faqs.q: Do I have to give a buyer Ohio's disclosure form?
faqs.a: Yes for houses of one to four units, subject to exceptions. A buyer who gets it after the contract is signed has three business days to rescind (Ohio Revised Code 5302.30).

faqs.q: Why does Medina Square have so many Victorian buildings?
faqs.a: The business district was destroyed by fire in 1848, and a second fire in 1870 destroyed 45 buildings. Rebuilding took almost ten years, and the Square is now a recognized historic district.

faqs.q: Where can I ask about building permits in Medina?
faqs.a: Call the city's Building Department at 330-722-9030. The department regulates construction and enforces property maintenance, and the Planning Department answers zoning questions.
